inputKind: Authored public source summaries, locators, limitations and case summaries with counterevidence. Full documents, private records and bank ledgers are not model inputs.
scope: Only the three regional catalogs and national-institution catalog retained in this release. Not a national representative sample or complete archive.
lineageLimitation: Case/source summaries and repeated sources are dependent descriptions; neither matching counts nor scores establish independent corroboration.

documents.title: National / Delhi: verify beneficial-control reporting after the FDI rule change
documents.text: Do the revised investment reports preserve the ownership aggregation and effective-control tests required by the Gazette? The August 21 government update reports 29 proposed investments worth₹4,895.65 crore under the revised framework. The public summary does not identify their investees. This is a national policy/control-monitoring case indexed at Delhi, not an allegation against those investors. The Gazette notification dated May 1 was published May 2,2026, with commencement on publication; PN 2 itself deferred commencement to FEMA notification. Cumulative direct/indirect rights, control over the investor and ultimate effective control over the investee remain explicit tests. A small nominal shareholding alone does not decide the route. The reported₹4,895.65 crore is proposed FDI across 29 reports as ofAugust 20, not certified incoming cash or expenditure. Counterevidence: Government states the purpose is clarity and faster lawful investment; the framework retains sector caps, control tests, reporting and prior approval for covered ownership changes. The Gazette expressly treats multilateral banks/funds of which India is a member differently for this rule. A World Bank or similar connection alone is not evidence of a prohibited route. Unvalidated scenario: A public government update distinguishes reported proposals from realized FDI under this specific amended framework by 2027-04-05. Alternatives: Long implementation lags can explain proposal/receipt differences. Confidentiality may limit investee detail; nonpublication does not establish evasion. Falsifiers: Same-regime aggregate data reconcile reported proposals, withdrawals and actual receipts. A proposed company-level theory fails exact-identity or effective-control checks.

documents.title: National / Delhi: follow the Navy lease beyond the signed contract
documents.text: Can the publicly announced foreign-supplier lease be reconciled to service acceptance, variation orders and payments? The August 17 MoD release names GA-ASI and a roughly ₹1,943 crore 30-month lease. Delhi is the signing/administration context; this is national procurement, not a Delhi incident or a corruption allegation. A signed contract is publicly reported for two systems for 30 months; the amount is a contract commitment, not a paid or lost amount. Additional Secretary and DG(Acquisition) A.Anbarasu is identified as present at signing; presence does not establish personal allocation, ownership or benefit. Counterevidence: MoD gives an operational capability purpose. The release contains no finding of overpricing, default or improper payment; different lease support bundles cannot be compared as bare aircraft unit prices. Unvalidated scenario: A public acceptance, contract-variation or audited-expenditure record for this exact August 17 lease becomes available by 2027-04-05. Alternatives: Normal contractual implementation can proceed without public operational detail. Different acquisition and leasing scopes can explain different headline amounts. Falsifiers: A linked acceptance/expenditure record reconciles the signed scope with paid milestones. A purported anomaly concerns a different contract, time period or support package.

documents.title: National / Delhi–Mumbai: reconcile write-offs with recovery cohorts
documents.text: Which public records can distinguish accounting write-offs, legally waived liabilities, settlements and actual recovery? A July 20 parliamentary reply answers a 15-year corporate-loan question using 12 FY rows for a different RBI reporting category. Delhi and Mumbai denote national policy and banking administration; the amounts are not city allocations. FY 2025–26 provisional Large–Industry & Services domestic figures are ₹15,213 crore written off and ₹4,456 crore actual recoveries. These annual flows are not a matched vintage. Separately, the March 31,2026 CRILC snapshot counts 1,249 borrowers with total written-off amounts of₹100 crore or more, totaling₹4,19,380 crore across all borrower types. The reply cites section 45 E confidentiality for borrower-level CRILC information; it does not supply names that can be joined to a minister or beneficiary. Counterevidence: The reply says write-off is an accounting procedure and borrower liabilities persist. Actual debt forgiveness, negotiated settlement and insolvency haircut need their own orders and cash records. Recoveries during a year can concern earlier write-offs; ratios of the two annual columns do not establish cohort recovery performance or personal benefit. Unvalidated scenario: RBI or DFS publishes a nonprovisional FY 2025–26 update of the same domestic Large–Industry & Services write-off/recovery categories by 2027-04-05. Alternatives: Category changes can explain differences without lost recoveries. A later publication may revise one measure only; missing matched cohorts prevent the proposed comparison. Falsifiers: Reconciled tables show category-consistent figures and explain revisions. A claim of a waiver lacks any legal discharge order and is only a write-off entry.

documents.text: Notification dated May 1 was published May 2 and takes effect on publication; amended rule 6 contains approval, ownership-change, reporting and cumulative-control rules. English text pp.3–5: rule 1(2), rule 6 provisos and Explanations 1–3 Official-URL full-text extract inspected through Exa; direct original download returned 503, so binary PDF identity is not verified. May 1 notification date and May 2 Gazette publication date are distinct. Multilateral banks/funds of which India is a member have a specific exception; foreignness alone is not evidence of an illicit route.

documents.text: Revises the land-border investment screening framework, retaining beneficial ownership, aggregated rights, control and reporting provisions; commencement depends on FEMA notification. documents.text: MoD reports a signed contract with GA-ASI for two systems for the Navy, approximately ₹1,943 crore over 30 months. Opening two substantive paragraphs Original government release retained; underlying executed agreement, price schedule and payments are not public in this packet. Contract value is not expenditure, unit aircraft purchase price or evidence of impropriety.

documents.title: Lok Sabha UQ 120: write-offs, recoveries and borrower disclosure scope
documents.text: The reply gives twelve FY rows for Large–Industry & Services domestic PSB write-offs and annual actual recoveries; it distinguishes accounting write-offs from waivers and describes confidentiality. Answer(a)–(d), FY 2014–15 through FY 2025–26 table, recovery caveat and CRILC table Read full extracted text from the official URL through Exa; direct PDF download returned 403, so original byte identity is not verified. This is not the requested full 15-year corporate-loan population. FY 2025–26 is provisional. Recoveries in a year can relate to other write-off vintages; do not compute a matched-cohort recovery rate. The separate 1,249 borrowers/₹4,19,380 crore CRILC snapshot covers all borrower types, not only the table’s large-industry category.

documents.title: Chandigarh: recurring Punjab procurement controls after PAC assurances
documents.text: Were prior PAC assurances converted into enforceable system controls and tender-level remedial decisions? The Punjab e-procurement audit compares 2018–2023 records with weaknesses reported in 2017. Chandigarh is the state administrative research hub, not the site of every audited tender. The new watch tests documented remediation rather than treating common credentials as proof of collusion. The audit analysed 1,85,920 tenders and examined 494 selected tenders across 111 procuring entities; the documentary sample and database population are different denominators. In the PWD first-instance single-bid cohort, 1130 tenders received one bid and 383 received awards; a separate 424 single-qualified-bid cohort produced 397 awards. These categories must not be assumed disjoint or summed as losses. Table 2.12 reports up to 214 registered bidders sharing an email, 83 a mobile number and 135 a PAN. These are maximum registrations per credential, not counts of proven collusive bidders. The chapter records the previous PAC assurance, missing automated single-bid restrictions, and aNovember 2024 advisory. That is a testable policy-to-system implementation gap. Counterevidence: The nodal department stated individual user departments made award decisions and said it issued an advisory. CAG considered an advisory insufficient because business rules needed system integration. Shared service providers or duplicate registrations may explain some credential overlap; exact legal identity and tender-specific conduct require separate evidence. Audit-era weaknesses are not verified current vulnerabilities. Unvalidated scenario: An action-taken record supplies testable evidence that single-bid and credential-verification controls or lawful exception processes were implemented. Alternatives: Rules allow documented exceptions. Controls have been implemented since the audited period. Falsifiers: Dated acceptance tests and sampled lawful exceptions demonstrate the cited gaps were remedied.

documents.title: CAG Uttarakhand report index: tabling 10 March 2026
documents.text: Official index identifies Dehradun Smart Cities Report 5 of 2025 as tabled 10 March 2026. Entry Report 5 of 2025 Index provides publication context, not an independent audit or current compliance assessment.

documents.title: Dehradun Smart City audit: execution and operation gaps
documents.text: Reporting confirms the audit’s asset-operation, consultant-payment and interdepartmental work-site problems. Project management and consultant-payment paragraphs Same underlying CAG audit. Does not establish all audited conditions persist inOctober 2026.

documents.title: Dehradun: paid smart assets, operating costs and recovery follow-through
documents.text: Were non-functional assets made operational and identified recoveries completed after management accepted the audit recommendations? The Smart Cities audit describes a measurable gap between capital spending and usable services, including school equipment without affordable electricity. It also documents successful water SCADA and other benefits. March 2026 tabling is recent disclosure of older expenditure; no fresh July–October remediation record was found. Against ₹737.50 crore released, ₹634.11 crore expenditure was reported for 2016–17 to 2022–23. These are programme totals, not irregularity totals. A ₹4.55 crore waste-monitoring module remained unused toFebruary 2025; ₹5.91 crore school smart equipment was non-functional because schools could not afford operating electricity. The summary records ₹5.19 crore consultant-payment irregularities and ₹19.06 crore unutilised agency funds not recovered, with distinct financial scopes. Counterevidence: CAG observed improved traffic and safety management and successful SCADA water-supply implementation; the entire programme was not a failure. Management agreed to all 12 recommendations. Work-site encumbrances and cross-department coordination contributed to delays, providing alternatives to corrupt-intent assumptions. Unvalidated scenario: A public compliance record documents recovered agency funds and funded operation of the audited school and waste-monitoring assets. Alternatives: Assets already restored after the audit snapshot. Operating budget and utility issues, not procurement fraud, explain outage. Falsifiers: Dated service logs and verified recovery vouchers demonstrate completed remediation.

documents.title: CAG Dehradun Smart Cities Mission executive summary
documents.text: Original summary identifies non-functional assets, consultant-payment controls and recoveries while recognising functioning SCADA and other benefits; management accepted all 12 recommendations. Executive summarypp v–viii Date is tabling date established by the official report index, not underlying expenditure date. Audit baseline 2017–18 to 2022–23 includes later updates such as February 2025; no July–October 2026 remediation record obtained.

documents.title: Delhi CAG flags GST, subsidy and procurement record gaps
documents.text: Reporting gives only 5363 award-of-contract records for approximately 155000 tenders and distinguishes expenditure, tax implications and subsidy findings. Paragraph beginning CAG also flagged deficiencies in Delhi’s e-procurement system Same underlying CAG audit as the Indian Express report; not an independent second audit. The rounded denominator and audit observation dates must not be treated as the current October 2026 portal population.

documents.title: Delhi CAG report: electricity subsidy and e-procurement findings
documents.text: Reporting on the audit tabled on 7 August 2026 describes shared bidder identifiers, subsidy eligibility questions, and an Assembly request for departmental action-taken notes. Sections Electricity subsidies and E-procurement system under scanner Original CAG report could not be retrieved from the inferred official URL; this source is reporting of an audit, not a court finding. Tender values are affected procurement scope, not proved losses. Shared IP addresses can have innocent explanations.

documents.title: Delhi: shared bidder credentials and missing award records
documents.text: Do documented bidder identifiers and missing award records survive legal-entity and transaction-level reconciliation? August 2026 reporting of a CAG audit identifies shared bidder identifiers and sparse award disclosure. The investigation tests bid independence and publication completeness; affected tender values are not corruption-loss estimates. Related subsidy and GST findings are separate financial populations. The reported 2017–18 to 2022–23 audit found 14,527 valid bids in 7,181 tenders valued at ₹3,217.44 crore sharing IP addresses; 45 tenders worth ₹530.25 crore involved common PAN registrations. These populations may overlap. Only 5,363 of approximately 155,000 tenders reportedly contained award details. Missing portal records do not prove no contract or missing expenditure. Subsidy findings include ₹17.81 crore for more than 50,000 connections showing zero consumption for more than a year. This is a distinct subsidy-control question, not a bidder-network payment. Counterevidence: Shared gateways, authorised filing agents and duplicate registration histories can explain some common identifiers; the inspected reporting does not identify final collusion findings or beneficiaries. The Assembly Speaker described PAC scrutiny and requested departmental action-taken notes; the inspected record does not establish their subsequent completion. Unvalidated scenario: A public PAC or departmental action-taken record reconciles at least one identified shared-credential tender cohort and its award notices. Alternatives: Common consultant or network gateway explains shared identifiers. Archived award files exist outside the portal. Falsifiers: Verified independent ownership, segregated bids and complete award/payment reconciliation resolve the selected cohort.

documents.title: Rajasthan HC denies Joshi and Agarwal bail in ACB proceeding
documents.text: Reports 13 August bail refusal, alleged certificate warnings and the court’s express trial-merits reservation. Opening paragraphs and certificate/payment discussion Original High Court order not acquired; reporting only. Bail refusal is not conviction. Sep 29 Supreme Court relief to Badaya and Dixit must not be applied automatically to Joshi or Agarwal.

documents.title: Jaipur: certificate warnings, tender approvals and alleged intermediaries
documents.text: Were qualification warnings received before approvals and alleged onward transfers, and can each claimed step survive the defence and original records? The 29 September 2026 Supreme Court bail order documents a prosecution theory involving qualification certificates, two contracting firms and an alleged intermediary route. It grants Badaya and Dixit bail and expressly leaves every factual allegation to trial. Joshi’s 2025 PMLA bail and 2026 ACB bail proceedings are tracked separately. SC paragraph 5 recites the allegation that Shri Ganpati Tubewell Company and Shri Shyam Tubewell Company used forged IRCON certificates to obtain approximately 104 tenders worth ₹979.45 crore. This is alleged contract scope, not quantified proven loss. SC paragraph 7(a) records an allegation that Shubhanshu Dixit failed to act on 2023 complaints while participating in finance-committee processes. His recorded office period is 30 December 2022 to 13 February 2024. SC paragraph 7(b) recites an alleged Badaya-mediated route through unnamed relatives/acquaintances to Sumangalam Landmark LLP; no account numbers, identities of unnamed people or transaction amounts are inferred. The 2025 PMLA order records the agency’s separate corporate-route account naming Mugdog Packaging India LLP, Maxclenz Retail PvtLtd and Jay The Victory before Sumangalam LLP. It does not establish pairwise transaction order, corporate identifiers or equivalence with the 2026 LLP label. Counterevidence: SC granted Badaya and Dixit bail on 29 September 2026: investigation against them complete, evidence seized, charges not yet framed and lengthy trial expected. Paragraph 18 disclaims any opinion on merits or evidentiary value. Joshi’s counsel said he caused suspensions, blacklisting and FIRs, disputed personal benefit, and said he was not a member of bid-evaluation or finance committees. These responses require checking against dated decision records. Joshi obtained PMLA bail 3 December 2025; reported ACB bail refusal 13 August 2026 is a distinct proceeding. Badaya/Dixit’sSeptember relief does not change Joshi’s ACB status; no later outcome was established by the cutoff search. Unvalidated scenario: A subsequent trial order records whether charges are framed and identifies the accepted qualification-certificate and financial-document issues. Alternatives: Warnings were investigated or authenticity clarified before award. Lawful independent commercial consideration explains a transfer. Agency characterisation or identity matching is disproved. Falsifiers: Certified records refute certificate falsity, establish adequate official action, or disprove the alleged transfer/identity step.

documents.title: Joshi counsel disputes tender-committee role in ACB bail hearing
documents.text: Records the defence argument that Joshi was not on the bid-evaluation or finance committee and challenges the timing of his ACB arrest; reports bail denial. Counsel Snehdeep response paragraphs Same 13 August hearing as Times of India; separate reporting does not create an independent evidentiary event. No later Joshi ACB merits outcome was established by searches through 7 October 2026.

documents.title: Sanjay Badaya and Shubhanshu Dixit v State of Rajasthan, 2026 INSC 1065
documents.text: Bail order recites prosecution allegations about forged qualification certificates and an intermediary route, grants bail to Badaya and Dixit, and expressly reserves every allegation and evidentiary issue for trial. Paragraphs 4–7 and 9–18 Publisher identity is Supreme Court; hosting is a third-party mirror, not an official-host verification. Paragraphs 5 and 7 are prosecution allegations, not judicial findings of fraud, payments or culpability. ₹979.45 crore is the alleged 104-tender contract scope, not proven loss.

documents.title: Mahesh Joshi v Directorate of Enforcement, bail order 3 December 2025
documents.text: The PMLA bail order records both the agency’s alleged corporate route and Joshi’s response that he initiated suspensions, blacklisting and FIRs; bail was granted without deciding merits. Order paragraphs 3,5–12,14–18; exclude editorial headnote Annotated third-party mirror; not an official-host verification. PMLA bail does not determine bail in the distinct ACB proceeding or establish innocence/guilt. Names are source mentions; the two variants Sumangalam LLP and Sumangalam Landmark LLP have not been merged through an LLPIN check.

documents.title: Lucknow: verify completed meter refunds and the replacement roadmap
documents.text: Did the regulator’s completed refund population omit eligible accounts, and will the no-cost replacement roadmap be filed? The August 27 regulatory disposal supersedes earlier stories of pending credits. The next test is reconciliation of 92,231 credited accounts, 907 exclusions and any omitted eligible connections, plus delivery of the required legacy-meter roadmap. The final reported reconciliation is 93,138 examined connections minus 907 non-overcharged STS accounts equals 92,231 credited eligible accounts, with ₹32.74 crore in the original paragraph 17 table and ₹32.75 crore in paragraph 22. The later news report matches the table. Both original values are retained; no exact reconciled total is asserted. Earlier 11 August proceedings described 6,188 still-uncredited accounts and missed filing deadlines; this earlier status must not be presented as current after the disposal order. Paragraph 21 directs a roadmap within two months for replacing all keypad/token meters, including 907 existing STS meters. Paragraph 20 quotes the 21 November 2025 tariff-order no-additional-cost requirement; paragraph 21 records UPPCL’s statement that 907 meters predated an order described there as 22 November 2025. The document’s one-day date discrepancy is preserved. Counterevidence: UPPCL attributed interim pricing to the absence of a revised cost-data book and invoked central smart-meter policy; the regulator rejected that as authority for the excess recovery. The case was disposed after reported credits and exclusion of 907 accounts that were not overcharged. No unresolved ₹33 crore balance should be fabricated. Order paragraphs 14–16 record UPPCL’s explanation that 373,509 connections was the gross Jhatpat population including non-smart meters, while 93,138 was the examined refund cohort. The larger total is not proof of omitted refunds. Unvalidated scenario: The required STS replacement roadmap is filed and the regulator records how remaining or newly identified eligible refunds are handled. Alternatives: Roadmap filed but not indexed online. Differences arise from genuinely different meter or connection populations. Falsifiers: Dated filing and anonymised complete reconciliation resolve all eligible accounts with verified exclusions.

documents.title: Bihar cabinet policy and vehicle procurement decisions
documents.text: A separately bylined report of the same cabinet briefing gives 30 water cannons at ₹88 lakh and 86 Vajra vehicles at ₹42 lakh; it records the government’s crowd-control and emergency rationale. Nod for water cannons section Article body publication date 1 OctoberIST retained; search metadata says 30 SeptemberUTC. Both are before the cutoff. Same cabinet decision, not an independent procurement audit; original cabinet memorandum still required.

documents.title: Bihar approves ₹62.52 crore of crowd-control vehicles
documents.text: Reports administrative approval for 30 water cannons and 86 Vajra vehicles, government use-case justification and falling reported riot counts. Opening approval paragraphs; Home Department response; final historical-count paragraph Administrative approval is not a tender award, invoice, delivery or expenditure. No winning supplier is established. Riot counts are only one demand indicator; festivals, emergencies, geography and fleet condition also matter.

documents.title: Patna: prospective watch on ₹62.52 crore police-vehicle approval
documents.text: Will the approved crowd-control vehicles have documented need, competitive awards, delivery verification and lifecycle-cost justification? The 30 September 2026 cabinet decision provides a prospective baseline before known awards: 30 water cannons and 86 Vajra vehicles. It is a procurement-monitoring case, with no evidence here of corrupt awards or named supplier benefits. Administrative approval totals ₹62.52 crore: 30× ₹88 lakh= ₹26.40 crore and 86× ₹42 lakh= ₹36.12 crore. The amounts are approval estimates, not verified payments. The Home Department cited festivals, rallies, VIP movements, riots and emergencies. The approval follows formation of district anti-riot units. Reported state riot counts declined from 9,419 in 2020 to 2,502 in 2025. That challenges a simplistic rising-riots justification but does not establish fleet requirements or misuse. Counterevidence: Fleet age, regional coverage, replacement needs and emergency duties can justify capacity despite falling incident counts. Neither inspected report provides inventory data or evidence of a tainted award. No vendor, tender outcome, disbursement or minister-to-company financial link is established; the graph stops at the administrative decision. Unvalidated scenario: A published tender or award for the approved fleet exposes quantities, specifications, selection method and a documented needs assessment. Alternatives: Legitimate technical safety standards narrow suppliers. Published estimates change through competitive price discovery or scope approval. Falsifiers: Open comparable competition, reasoned needs and compliant delivery/payment records explain the procurement.

Final-data and concluding roadmap paragraphs Same regulatory proceeding; the article’s ₹32.74 crore matches the original paragraph 17 table, while paragraph 22 states ₹32.75 crore. documents.text: Earlier report describes 6,188 pending accounts and a 93,138-account initial population, interim rate justification and the regulator’s demand for full credits. Its paragraph 17 table totals ₹32.74 crore while paragraph 22 states ₹32.75 crore. Both are retained; exact unrounded reconciliation is unacquired.
